articles.title: Lord’s Mark Industries’ Brahmastra puts Indian defence innovation on the global stage
articles.summary: Lord’s Mark Industries Limited is working to strengthen India’s position in the global defence technology landscape through indigenous innovation.
articles.body: Lord’s Mark Industries Limited is working to strengthen India’s position in the global defence technology landscape through indigenous innovation. Guided by its focus on technology and the Make in India vision, the company began this journey three years ago with the aim of developing world-class defence technologies that reflect India’s engineering capabilities and have relevance beyond the domestic market.This strategic foresight reflects management’s ambition to move beyond conventional manufacturing, develop proprietary technologies on Indian soil and build the foundation for a potential global monopoly in these specialised product categories. With three years of focused R&D behind its flagship innovations, Brahamastra is now positioned to explore international markets and demonstrate the capabilities of Indian engineering on the global stage.Brahamastra’s showcased portfolio includes three flagship products—BRAK RT, a long-range laser rangefinder with a day-channel camera; BRAK Alpha, a multipurpose laser rangefinder; and TRC-1, a smart trail camerawith no equivalent products available anywhere else in the world. The company’s wider portfolio also includes holographic and reflex sights, telescopic sights, thermal imaging sights, handheld thermal imagers, day/night surveillance systems, anti-drone systems and other optoelectronic equipment. Its core focus is on advancing indigenous defence manufacturing in line with the Atmanirbhar Bharat initiative.The BRAK RT combines laser-based distance measurement with a dedicated day-observation camera in a single instrument. Its stated specifications include a maximum measuring range of 20,000 metres, distance accuracy of up to one metre (1σ), and the ability to detect up to five targets. Integrated GPS and orientation sensors provide positional and directional information, while its IP68-rated construction is designed for demanding environmental conditions1.BRAK Alpha is a multipurpose laser rangefinder designed to combine distance measurement with target detection and orientation data. It offers a stated measurement range of 10–5,000 metres, accuracy of up to 0.5 metres (1σ), and detection of up to five targets. GPS, azimuth measurement and inclination sensing further support its field-use capabilities2.The TRC-1 Smart Trail Camera combines motion-triggered imaging with day-and-night capture for field-surveillance applications. Its stated specifications include 5 MP or higher still images, 1080p video, a minimum 120-degree field of view and invisible infrared illumination up to 10 metres. Developed and manufactured in Navi Mumbai, Maharashtra, the product also incorporates a management concept featuring role-based permissions and audit records, with video intended to remain on the camera rather than being centrally stored by the management platform3.A growing market opportunityThe investment also positions Brahamastra to pursue opportunities in a growing defence technology market. According to MarketsandMarkets4, India’s military electro-optics and infrared (EO/IR) market is projected to grow from US1.19billionin2026toUS1.78 billion by 2030, registering a CAGR of 10.4%. The growth is supported by increasing requirements for night operations, border surveillance and target detection, alongside modernisation across land, air and naval platforms.Globally, the military electro-optical and infrared systems market is projected to expand from US9.09 billion in 2025 to US 10.77 billion by 2031, at a CAGR of 2.87%, according to Mordor Intelligence5. Demand for advanced sensors, optics, long-range targeting and surveillance technologies is creating opportunities for specialised product developers. These market trends offer Brahamastra a potential pathway to explore international partnerships, product deployment and export opportunities, subject to applicable technical qualifications, regulatory requirements and procurement processes.Commenting on the strategic vision behind the investment, Dr Sachidanand Upadhyay, Founder, MD & CEO of Lord’s Mark Industries Limited, said: “Our love and enthusiasm for technology and belief in the Make in India vision led us to embark on this journey three years ago. We saw an opportunity to harness India’s engineering talent and research capabilities to develop world-class indigenous defence technologies with global relevance. Our vision has always been to go beyond fulfilling domestic needs and create products that reflect India’s technological strength on the international stage. Brahamastra’s evolving portfolio is a step in that direction, with the potential to open new markets and establish India as a recognised contributor to specialised defence technology.”With its investment in Brahamastra Defence Techno Products Limited, Lord’s Mark Industries Limited is pursuing a long-term strategy centred on indigenous research, advanced product development and global market opportunities. By developing specialised technologies within India, the company aims to contribute to the country’s defence manufacturing capabilities while creating a platform for Brahamastra to explore international markets and demonstrate the strength of Indian engineering on the global stage.For more details, visit the official website.References: Disclaimer - The above content is non-editorial, and TIL hereby disclaims any and all warranties, expressed or implied, relating to it, and does not guarantee, vouch for or necessarily endorse any of the content.You use AI every day. articles.title: Mumbai Airport proposes flights to 14 international destinations of all airlines to operate from Navi Mumbai from next summer; sends plan to govt
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: International flights to and from 14 destinations of all - Indian and foreign - airlines could be shifted out of Mumbai's Chhatrapati Shivaji
articles.body: NEW DELHI: International flights to and from 14 destinations of all - Indian and foreign - airlines could be shifted out of Mumbai's Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport (CSMIA) by next summer and operate only from Navi Mumbai Int'l Airport (NMIA).The Adani Group, which operates both these Mumbai Metropolitan Region (MMR) airports, plans to do this as Indian carriers -- Air India Group, IndiGo and Akasa -- have agreed to move some of their international flights to NMIA from CSMIA over the next few months while foreign carriers are yet to agree to do so.The 14 destinations are Bahrain, Dammam, Dhaka, Doha, Fujairah, Jakarta, Jeddah, Kathmandu, Kuwait City, Madinah, Muscat, Ras Al Khaimah, Riyadh and Sharjah.Mumbai International Airport Ltd (MIAL) needs to urgently start demolition of the decades old terminal 1 as parts of it have been deemed structurally unsafe in technical studies. For that it needs airlines to shift flights to NMIA so that demolition of T1 can begin and a new terminal be built in its place.There have been multiple meetings between airlines and MIAL - which plans to begin T1 demolition next April - on the issue. Mumbai airport needs to shift 50 lakh passengers annually to NMIA. Their agreement with Indian carriers takes care of 30 lakh and still leaves 20 lakh.To achieve this, MIAL is learnt to have written to Union aviation secretary Samir Sinha that unless (foreign) airlines get on board, it plans that all flights to and from the 14 destinations identified by Indian carriers for shifting will operate at NMIA for all airlines.MIAL had asked airlines to tell latest by Nov 3 which slots will they temporarily vacate at CSMIA for the next summer season that starts March end.It is learnt to have requested the aviation ministry that if airlines don't revert on the same, it plans to implement the 14-foreign-destinations-from-NMIA plan. Sources say these cities have been chosen to ensure all MMR connectivity to them is at NMIA to minimise confusion among passengers.The aviation ministry is going to consider this and take a decision after taking into account all factors.You use AI every day. articles.title: Kraft Heinz to Sell Coffee Unit to Refocus on Other Brands
articles.summary: Kraft Heinz Co. said Wednesday it was divesting its North American coffee business in a bid to tighten its portfolio as the company seeks to jump start its g...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Kraft Heinz Co. ( KHC ) said Wednesday it was divesting its North American coffee business in a bid to tighten its portfolio as the company seeks to jump start its growth.

Under the proposed transaction, Kraft Heinz is unloading a slew of coffee brands including Maxwell House and Gevalia, to private equity firm One Rock Capital Partners, LLC at an enterprise value of $650 million. Kraft Heinz will keep a 30% non-controlling equity stake in the coffee unit. The deal is expected to close in mid-2027, the company said.

The maker of Kraft Mac & Cheese and Heinz ketchup has been working to revive some of its struggling brands with more resources. Divesting the coffee business will allow those funds to be more effective, the company said Wednesday.

"This transaction is a meaningful step in unlocking value from our portfolio and will further accelerate the momentum behind our transformation," Chief Executive Officer Steve Cahillane said in a statement.

The divestment is one of the company's biggest moves this year to refocus its attention on brands it believes it can revitalize, while disentangling itself from others. Coffee has seen increased competition from energy drinks in recent years, though it remains a huge global market.

Shares of Kraft Heinz rose 3% at 7:17 am in premarket trading Wednesday in New York.

The company also reported third-quarter adjusted earnings per share of 53 cents that came in above the average of analysts' expectations. Kraft Heinz also raised the low end of its organic revenue outlook for the full 2026 year to -1.25% to -0.5%, up from a low end of -2% previously.

Earlier this year, Cahillane halted the company's plans to split into two entities, saying the food maker could be revitalized with a $700 million infusion into marketing, better deals and research and development.

Cahillane said Wednesday that market share, sales, and volume trends are improving in every region, compared with the previous year.

The net cash proceeds after taxes of the deal are expected to be around $500 million, which the company said will be used to pay down debt. Around 250 Kraft Heinz employees will transition with the coffee business, the company said.

articles.title: Block stock jumps as Jack Dorsey's AI bet shows signs of paying off
articles.summary: Eight months after Jack Dorsey made one of corporate America's boldest bets on shrinking its workforce to prepare for the age of artificial intelligence, inv...
articles.body:
Eight months after Jack Dorsey made one of corporate America's boldest bets on shrinking its workforce to prepare for the age of artificial intelligence, investors are finding more reasons to buy into the Silicon Valley billionaire's pivot.

Shares of Dorsey's Block ( XYZ ), the payments company behind Cash App and merchant processor Square, jumped 15% in Wednesday morning trading after it reported better-than-expected third quarter earnings and raised its gross profit outlook for next year.

If the move lasts through Wednesday trading, it will mark the stock's best one-day performance since investors embraced co-founder and CEO Dorsey's somewhat controversial decision in February to let go of 40% of Block's workforce.

The company gave more evidence of the financial benefits from its sweeping overhaul Tuesday afternoon. Gross profit at Block rose 22% in the third quarter from a year ago to $3.2 billion, while adjusted operating income surged 92% to $923 million as Block benefited from lower personnel costs.

Block's sweeping restructuring move this year has raised questions over whether AI advancements were genuinely allowing the payments company to operate with close to half as many employees or whether enthusiasm for the technology provided cover for the company to initiate a sweeping cost-cutting exercise after years of over hiring.

The Oakland, California based company's third quarter results delivered some evidence of its savings from a smaller workforce. Adjusted product development expenses fell 12% from a year ago. The company also said AI is taking over a growing number of routine software tasks but it didn't disclose how much of its improved operating profits can be tied directly to the technology.

Block's core business also showed some momentum in the quarter. Cash App reached 60 million monthly transacting users in September after hovering between 58 million to 59 million for the past four quarters. Block's merchant processer unit, Square, also reported gross payment volume rose by 14% year over year compared to 13% in the previous quarter.

The company projected total gross profit next year to be $14.52 billion, or roughly $110 million ahead of Wall Street's expectations, according to BTIG.

"We believe we've meaningfully crossed the chasm of transforming our company from one that creates traditional financial products into one that streams intelligence as people need it," Dorsey wrote in Block's third quarter shareholder letter.

Executives also provided more details on Block's artificial intelligence strategy, with Dorsey highlighting how Block plans to turn some of the AI tools it has developed into new sources of revenue.

articles.title: Ángel, de 32 años, propietario de 12 pisos en alquiler que le generan 5.500 euros al mes: “Hago lo que quiero cuando quiero”
articles.standfirst: Empezó con 30.000 euros ahorrados y ahora quiere ser promotor
articles.summary: Empezó con 30.000 euros ahorrados y ahora quiere ser promotor
articles.body: Un chalet con garaje, sin horarios ni jefe y con el alquiler pagado por sus propios inquilinos. Así vive hoy un joven de Valladolid que hace solo seis años era un asalariado más. Se llama Ángel, tiene 32 años y ya es dueño de 12 viviendas en alquiler que le dejan unos 5.500 euros al mes, según ha contado en el canal de YouTube Libertad Inmobiliaria. Su historia empezó a los 26 años, cuando trabajaba por cuenta ajena. Había ahorrado 30.000 euros y pensaba gastarlos en un coche, pero cambió de idea tras hacer algunos cursos de bolsa y darse cuenta de que el dinero podía generar más dinero. Para lograrlo, renunció a salir y a darse ciertos caprichos. Su primer piso lo compró en un pueblo de Valladolid por menos de 48.000 euros, con un préstamo personal y una rentabilidad cercana al 9,5 %. Desde entonces, su método ha sido siempre el mismo: comprar barato, reformar y alquilar. Lo más llamativo es que Ángel vive de alquiler. Este año se ha mudado a un chalet con garaje por el que paga 1.400 euros al mes, y asegura que esa cuota la cubren las rentas de dos de sus pisos. Gracias a ello no depende de una nómina y puede organizar su tiempo como quiere, hasta el punto de irse a esquiar un martes. Su última compra es un piso de tres habitaciones en el barrio de la Rondilla. Lo ha conseguido por 95.000 euros, cuando en el mercado rondaba los 120.000, y le dedicará 12.000 euros de reforma para alquilarlo por unos 800 euros al mes. Invierte en Valladolid por su cercanía a Madrid, su industria y unos precios todavía contenidos. Ahora quiere dar el salto a promotor. Ha comprado un edificio con cinco viviendas antiguas que convertirá en 14 apartamentos de una y dos habitaciones. Su consejo para quien quiera seguir sus pasos es sencillo: hacer números, perder el miedo y lanzarse si la operación sale bien.

articles.title: Trump tariff taxes Republicans: What US midterm results mean for Indian H-1B visa holders, Russian oil & trade deal
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has suffered a major blow in midterm elections with Republicans losing control of both the House of Representatives and the
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has suffered a major blow in midterm elections with Republicans losing control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.In a significant rebuke to Trump, American voters on Tuesday handed control of the US Congress to the opposition Democratic Party and shifted several key gubernatorial positions in closely watched elections.Trump's Republican Party suffered major defeats in its strongholds, including Texas, Georgia and Iowa, losing the governors' offices to Democratic candidates.Trump’s policies are being blamed by many as the reason for the loss - with tariffs and inflation in focus.The results are expected to have implications extending beyond the US - so what does this mean for India? Let’s take a look:What it means for H-1B visa holders and green card aspirantsUS President Donald Trump has tightened access to H-1B visas through a $100,000 fee and a wage-weighted selection system, making it harder for Indian professionals to secure US jobs. His administration has also suspended eight technology companies from the PERM green card programme, disrupting some workers’ routes to permanent residency and green cards. So will the midterm results change that attitude?No. Not much is expected to change on this front, despite Trump’s loss. This is because both Democrats and Republicans prioritise domestic employment.According to Ajay Srivastava, founder of Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), tighter immigration policies find bipartisan support.“Be it the Biden administration or the Trump one, policies are increasingly becoming restrictive and that approach is unlikely to change,” Srivastava tells TOI.Also Read | ‘Death by restriction’: As Trump sours H-1B visa dream, which Indian IT professionals face the biggest hit?According to Rajiv Dabhadkar, Founder, National Organization For Software and Technology Professionals, the H-1B debate has moved beyond party politics to a fundamental US policy challenge: protecting American jobs while retaining access to global talent.“Regardless of the outcome of the midterm elections, the US is looking to address long-standing flaws in the immigration system, including wage protections, worker displacement and how employers use foreign professionals,” he tells TOI.What fundamentally needs to be understood is that H-1B reform is now a bipartisan American policy imperative, not merely a political reaction to one administration, he adds.India’s purchase of Russian oilEarlier this year, the Donald Trump administration managed to get support for the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. The Act allows the US President to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries importing oil from Russia and Iran in a big way.India and China lead the lot of Russian oil buyers. Recently, Trump announced a waiver on those tariffs for India. But, it’s important to note that the waiver was only for a period of 60 days.Also Read | Does Trump’s 60-day tariff waiver really give relief to India? What it means for US trade deal & oil pricesThe Republicans losing control of the Congress is unlikely to change the Trump administration’s stance on buyers of Russian crude oil. This is because the bill enjoyed bipartisan support - both Democrats and Republicans appear keen to penalise buyers of Russian oil.However, what may work in India’s favour for now is America’s own diesel deal with Russia and the need by the Trump administration and even the Democrats to keep oil prices in check. Sanctioning Russian oil or penalising buyers of Moscow’s crude will not help that cause.So, for now India continues to enjoy relief from the prospect of 100% tariffs for its crude oil procurement from Russia, but this may work as a pressure tactic by the US to finalise a trade deal.India-US trade deal & tariffsFor India, which is still negotiating a trade agreement with the United States, the outcome of the midterm elections could strengthen the case for taking a cautious, wait-and-watch approach.Earlier this month, Commerce minister Piyush Goyal said the first phase of the India-US trade agreement was in the final stages of drafting. However, he stressed that New Delhi would move ahead only if the terms gave Indian exporters an edge over their competitors.India and the US have already finalised a framework for the first phase of the Bilateral Trade Agreement. However, changes in the US tariff environment have led to further negotiations. India is seeking tariff rates on its exports that are more favourable than those faced by competing countries.In the meantime, experts believe the midterm setback could prompt Trump to pursue an early trade agreement with India. They said that with Washington struggling to exercise foreign policy leverage over Russia, China and Iran, Trump may look for quick success on the trade front.However, the economic think tank GTRI said the unfavourable midterm outcome was unlikely to fundamentally alter Trump's trade policy. Both Republicans and Democrats, it noted, support economic nationalism, domestic manufacturing and robust supply chains."With foreign policy leverage failing against Russia, China, and Iran, Trump needs a quick win. Expect heightened pressure on India for a trade deal to prove American clout and the midterm losses may push Trump to seek a quick India trade deal," said Ajay Srivastava.Federation of Indian Export Organisations (FIEO) president SC Ralhan said the US continues to be an important destination for Indian goods and services."What will matter to Indian exporters in the months ahead is how US policy on tariffs and market access takes shape. MSMEs in particular need predictable trading conditions to price orders confidently and plan shipments months in advance," he told PTI.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. According to the company, developed to address diverse requirements across the galvanizing value chain, the alloys are designed to enhance process efficiency, improve coating consistency and strengthen long-term performance of galvanized steel.According to a 2026 CII–Nomura Research Institute report, corrosion related losses in India are estimated at approximately 4.3% of the country’s GDP annually. By enabling better control of aluminium levels in galvanising baths, the alloy supports stable bath chemistry, uniform coating thickness and improved surface finish.VedAyush, a specialised zinc-aluminium-magnesium alloy, is engineered to enhance corrosion protection, durability and coating performance across demanding industrial environments. articles.title: Pistachios vanish from Diwali gift boxes as prices nearly double, almond rates also up 20%; companies add seeds and berries as dry fruit costs jump 25-40%
articles.summary: Your dry fruits box this Diwali may look very different!
articles.body: Your dry fruits box this Diwali may look very different! With the cost of dry fruits going up, retailers are looking at alternatives to fill in the boxes this time.For example, pistachios are becoming increasingly scarce in Diwali gift hampers this year as a steep rise in prices and supply constraints force companies and retailers to look for cheaper alternatives, including seeds and berries.Almond quantities are also being cut to keep gifting costs under control. Despite these changes, sales volumes of dry fruit and nut gift packs have grown 5-7% year-on-year, according to industry executives.Pistachios prices almost doubleRetail prices of pistachios have almost doubled compared with a year ago, driven by supply disruptions associated with the West Asia conflict and a smaller US crop. Almond prices, meanwhile, have climbed around 20%, according to dry fruit processors and importers.At the premium end of the gifting market, however, demand for exotic nuts such as pecans, macadamias and hazelnuts remains on the rise.Flavoured cashews are also gaining popularity, industry executives told ET. Industry estimates suggest that 30-35% of India's annual nuts and dry fruits sales, valued at an estimated Rs 75,000 crore, take place around Diwali.“Pistachio have been the game spoiler this year. The prices of pistachio from all origins including Iran, Afghanistan and California have increased,” said Ravindra Mehta, member of central governing council at Nuts and Dry Fruits Council of India (NDFC-I).“The current pistachio crop in California is expected to be only about 40% of last year, which has led to an increase of 50% in pista prices in the wholesale markets and even more in retail,” he told the financial daily.Dry fruit prices on the riseThe price increase has extended beyond pistachios and almonds. The overall basket of nuts and dry fruits has become 25-40% more expensive year-on-year, importers, wholesalers and retailers said.Factors behind the rise include weather-related disruptions that have reduced global output, higher shipping expenses, lower supplies from Iran and Afghanistan, and the rupee's depreciation.With pistachios becoming harder to source and almonds being rationed in gift packs, companies have also started cutting the total weight of their hampers.Mehta said the reduction in the weight of dry fruit gift packs was unprecedented. Although pistachios were being replaced with less expensive alternatives, almonds, cashews and raisins remained essential components of such hampers. With corporate gifting budgets fixed, reducing the quantity of dry fruits was one way to keep costs within the allocated limits.Despite rising prices and changes in the composition of gift boxes, demand has remained strong.Rahul Kamath, director at Bola Agro, India's largest cashew processor, said Diwali sales of nuts and dry fruits had grown by around 5-7% year-on-year, whether measured through overall sales or sales at existing stores. articles.title: CVS announces plan to split into 2 companies, stock sinks 10%
articles.summary: CVS announced plans to separate into two independent, publicly traded companies on Wednesday, reshaping one of the largest healthcare companies in the US.
articles.body:
CVS Health Corporation ( CVS ) announced plans on Wednesday to separate into two independent, publicly traded companies, reshaping one of the largest healthcare companies in the US.

Shares of CVS dropped roughly 10% on Wednesday. The company also reported quarterly results.

CVS Health intends to separate its insurance, pharmacy benefit management, and healthcare services operations from its retail pharmacy and community healthcare segments.

The planned split marks a major shift from CVS Health's long-term strategy to bring together insurance, pharmacy benefit management, and healthcare services under one single structure.

Under the proposed plan, one company will retain the CVS Health name and house Aetna, CVS Caremark, CVS Specialty, Oak Street Health, and Signify Health.

The second entity will operate under the name CVS Pharmacy. It will include approximately 9,000 retail pharmacy locations and MinuteClinic locations, among other services.

Management believes separating the businesses will allow each organization to operate with greater independence while maintaining the ability to pursue partnerships across the healthcare industry.

The planned separation is expected to be completed in the first half of 2028.

On Wednesday, CVS also reported third quarter results with total revenue increasing 5.4% year over year to $108.4 billion, compared with $102.9 billion in the prior-year period. Adjusted earnings per share rose to $2.09 from $1.60 a year earlier.

Following the quarterly performance, CVS raised its full-year 2026 financial guidance, now expecting adjusted earnings per share of at least $8.20, compared with its previous range of $7.90 to $8.10.

articles.title: Suppliers to street vendors may inflate bills if hit by MDR: ISB study
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Although most UPI transactions fall outside the proposed merchant discount rate (MDR) framework, suppliers to street vendors could face charges on
articles.body: MUMBAI: Although most UPI transactions fall outside the proposed merchant discount rate (MDR) framework, suppliers to street vendors could face charges on payments exceeding Rs 2,000, prompting many vendors to consider passing on the additional cost to customers or switching to cash, according to a survey by the Indian School of Business (ISB).The study, conducted by ISB's Centre for Analytical Finance (CAF), found that nearly 70% of street vendors make supplier payments exceeding Rs 2,000, bringing these transactions within the proposed MDR threshold. About 10.4% of respondents said suppliers had demanded additional charges for UPI payments in the 10 days before the survey. All respondents said they would switch to cash if suppliers imposed such charges.The survey of 722 street vendors across 14 states and UTs and 64 urban local bodies found that 67% accepted UPI payments, but only 52% were aware of the proposed MDR framework. Adoption was highest in Tier 1 cities at 82%, compared with 66% in Tier 2 and 64% in Tier 3 cities.Awareness of the proposed charges was also higher among Tier 1 vendors at 66%, compared with 55% in Tier 2 and 47% in Tier 3. Among vendors accepting UPI, 64% knew about the proposed charges, against 26% of those who did not use the payment system. However, awareness did not necessarily translate into an understanding of the framework's applicability. Among vendors aware of MDR, 48% in Tier 1, 46% in Tier 2 and 33% in Tier 3 believed the charges would apply to them.The prospect of additional costs could also affect digital payment adoption. Around 53% of Tier 1 vendors and 45% each in Tier 2 and Tier 3 said they would reduce UPI acceptance if MDR were imposed.The survey also found that some vendors might pass on the charges to customers despite regulations prohibiting merchants from adding MDR to customer bills. Around 30% of Tier 1 vendors, 14% in Tier 2 and 19% in Tier 3 said they would do so.The impact was more pronounced among vendors who had already faced supplier surcharges. Of these, 30.8% said they would pass on the additional cost to customers, compared with 16.2% among those who had not faced such charges.CAF cautioned that exemptions for small merchants at the retail level may not shield them from costs arising during wholesale procurement. Supplier surcharges could squeeze vendors' margins, encourage cash transactions and weaken digital payment adoption, transaction transparency and access to formal credit.The centre recommended limited pilot studies before wider implementation, with monitoring of supplier charges, changes in customer pricing and shifts towards cash. It also called for an independent assessment of UPI operating costs to guide decisions on how these should be shared.Announced in Sept 2026, the proposed framework provides for a 0.4% charge on transactions above Rs 2,000 while exempting small merchants receiving up to Rs 1 lakh a month through QR payments. NPCI postponed the planned Oct 15 rollout until after Diwali. A fresh implementation date is yet to be announced.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Why the Democrat blue wave could be a good thing for Apple stock
articles.summary: Apple is seen as an early winner from the Blue Wave.
articles.body:
True to form, Wall Street is wasting no time picking winners and losers from the fresh Democratic blue wave that washed through the midterm elections late Wednesday.

One winner could be Apple ( AAPL ) for two reasons, Evercore ISI analyst Amit Daryanani opined.

The first is more of a defensive play amid the unknown that is fresh D.C. gridlock.

"Apple offers a different earnings driver through iPhone mix/pricing and services rather than data-center construction; our work points to resilient demand, with gross-margin recovery and price elasticity the key tests. This is THE name to keep working when investors want to get defensive," Daryanani said.

The other aspect is cooling memory chip prices, a major headwind for Apple, as data center projects get delayed or outright blocked by the Dems.

Daryanani added, "Memory input inflation (DRAM & NAND) has been a sizable headwind for a host of names in our coverage (AAPL for example, talked about 140bps GM headwind in Dec-qtr due to memory, but also PC names). Could a slowdown in DC buildouts actually temper memory demand and, in a way, help companies that have been impacted by the sizable memory inflation (AAPL is the key one but there are many others)?"

Apple stock rose 6% on Wednesday to touch a new all-time high.

The midterm election results threaten to significantly disrupt AI data center expansion as voter backlash over soaring utility bills, grid instability, and water usage drives a sharp political pivot toward tighter regulatory oversight.

In Texas, a dramatic political shift saw James Talarico capture a US Senate seat and Gina Hinojosa oust Greg Abbott in the gubernatorial race. This brings unprecedented scrutiny to ERCOT's independent grid allocations and unchecked tech consumption.

Paired with Senate wins by Roy Cooper in North Carolina and Sherrod Brown in Ohio, along with Amy Acton's win for Ohio governor, these victories signal that the era of friction-free, subsidized hyperscaler build-outs could come to an abrupt end.

"Ohio, Texas and Georgia and that has implications for the AI trade and data center buildout. In the end — voters delivered a clear warning to the AI buildout: the money may be available, but local permission to build is becoming harder to secure and project delays can shift the timing of the spending but it does NOT eliminate the demand," Slatestone Wealth chief market strategist Kenny Polcari said.

articles.title: SpaceX and Tesla 'need to find the path forward with Texas' on the back of midterm 'Blue Wave'
articles.summary: Tesla (TSLA) and SpaceX (SPCX) stock fell on Wednesday after Democrats took control of both houses of Congress in a "Blue Wave" that flipped Texas, home to b...
articles.body:
Tesla ( TSLA ) and SpaceX ( SPCX ) stock fell on Wednesday after Democrats took control of both houses of Congress in a "Blue Wave" that flipped Texas, home to both companies, with potential implications for CEO Elon Musk.

Musk spent $224 million backing Texas Republicans, including $158 million in September alone, per The New York Times , part of at least $446 million he gave to Republican candidates and groups before the vote. Democrat Gina Hinojosa unseated Gov. Greg Abbott to become the first Democratic governor of Texas since 1990, and Democrat James Talarico beat Republican Ken Paxton for the Senate seat.

Tesla and SpaceX both dropped by over 2% despite the broad market rally, which includes Big Tech.

"Both of these stocks have major headline risk if we get a blue sweep," Vikram Rai of FirstNew York told Bloomberg ahead of the election.

Tesla's Austin gigafactory, its robotaxi service in multiple Texas cities, and SpaceX's Starbase launch site all sit under a Democratic governor. SpaceX moved its headquarters from California to Texas in 2024.

In Washington, a Democratic Congress could bring added scrutiny of Tesla's autonomous driving operations and SpaceX's government and national security contracts.

Hinojosa has also pledged a moratorium on new data center construction in the state, a move that threatens the AI buildout underpinning both stocks.

Then there's the merger. Reports suggest a push to announce a Tesla-SpaceX deal by the first half of 2027 so it can close while President Trump is still in office, though talks remain exploratory. Rai said Democrats can't block a deal on their own but could slow it down.

"The bigger thing is the rumored merger, right? So if Tesla and SpaceX now potentially can't merge, and that was the plan … or kind of priced into the market. I think that that draws some volatility too," Defiance ETFs CIO Sylvia Jablonski said to Yahoo Finance.

Wedbush's Dan Ives, a longtime bull on both companies, wrote that Musk "needs to find the path forward with Texas now with a Democratic win on both the Senate and Governor race."

Separately, SpaceX is pushing forward with its mobile ambitions, inking a deal with Qualcomm to secure 5G chips for a terrestrial network. Though bullish on SpaceX, any moves in the telecom space also face regulatory scrutiny.

Pras Subramanian is the lead mobility reporter for Yahoo Finance. You can follow him on X and on Instagram .

articles.title: AMD stock flat following strong Q3 earnings beat, as data center revenue climbs 97%
articles.summary: AMD beat expectations on the top and bottom lines.
articles.body:
AMD ( AMD ) stock was flat after the company reported better-than-anticipated top and bottom lines Q3 results after the Tuesday.

The company said its data center revenue exploded 97% year-over-year driven by server sales.

"Demand for our Instinct and EPYC products continued to strengthen, and we expect growth to accelerate further in the fourth quarter as we scale Helios and 'Venice' production," CEO Lisa Su said in a statement.

"With our leadership product portfolio and deep customer and supply chain relationships, we are confident in our ability to sustain very strong revenue growth and expanding profitability over the coming years."

For the quarter, AMD saw earnings per share (EPS) of $2.09 on revenue of $13.38 billion. Analysts were projecting EPS of $1.97 on revenue of $13.08 billion, according to Bloomberg consensus estimates.

The company saw EPS and revenue of $1.20 and $9.2 billion, respectively, in the same period last year.

AMD's Data Center arm generated sales of $8.5 billion, ahead of estimates of $8.19 billion. It reported revenue of $4.34 billion in the same period last year.

AMD's Client business revenue, which includes PC sales, hit $2.9 billion. Wall Street was looking for $3.06 billion.

The chipmaker's gaming business sales, however, came in at $773 million, down 40% year over year. Analysts were estimating revenue of $655 million.

The company's gaming division includes products ranging from PC graphics cards to custom silicon for game consoles. Both categories are facing higher prices due to the ongoing memory and storage shortage, depressing customer demand.

AMD's report comes after rival Intel reported better-than-anticipated Q3 results , but issued guidance well below analysts' projections last week. The news sent Intel stock plummeting nearly 29% .

The company blamed the outlook on a worse-than-anticipated decline in the PC market.

The industry is contending with two overlapping factors: difficult comparisons to last year, when Microsoft ended support for Windows 10, forcing enterprises to purchase newer Windows 11 systems, and the steady increase in PC prices, which is eating into demand.

articles.title: Duolingo stock soars over 30% on strong user growth, monetization plans
articles.summary: Duolingo stock shot 33% higher after the company reported a surge in daily active users and raised its financial guidance.
articles.body:
Duolingo ( DUOL ) stock rocketed 31% higher after the company reported a surge in daily active users and raised its financial guidance.

In the third quarter, Duolingo reported that its daily active users (DAUs) rose 29% year over year to 64.9 million. Paid subscribers for the language learning platform grew 14% annually to 13.1 million.

Investors also cheered management's note that the company will be "gradually leaning more into monetization in ways that preserve the quality of our free experience."

For Q3, Duolingo also beat Wall Street estimates on the top and bottom lines. Revenue came in at $309 million, up 12% year over year, versus analyst estimates of $303 million, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. Earnings per share of $0.58 also surpassed estimates of $0.56.

The company is eyeing even stronger user growth as it aims for 1 billion users. Duolingo said its operating expenses increased 24% year over year. Those expenses included $11.4 million that the company set aside for a company-wide performance bonus for employees if it achieves DAU growth of 25% or greater in Q4.

Duolingo raised its outlook across the board. For 2026, revenue is expected at $1.22 billion, ahead of the Street's forecast of $1.2 billion.

"We expect to finish 2026 at the high end of both the 10% to 12% bookings growth and 15% to 18% revenue growth targets we set at the start of the year," the company stated. "We expect full-year Adjusted EBITDA of $323 million, or a 26.5% margin, up $3 million from our previous guidance, and $21 million above the midpoint of our original 2026 guidance provided in February."

The quarter and market reaction on Wednesday went a long way toward patching up what's been a rough year for the stock. Year to date, Duolingo stock remains down 2%, versus a 12% gain for the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ).

"In our view, the quarter begins to address the primary investor concern following second-quarter results: whether accelerating engagement can translate into stronger monetization," William Blair analysts led by Ralph Schackart wrote in a note. "DAU growth accelerated for a second consecutive quarter, subscription bookings reaccelerated meaningfully, and management expects paid-subscriber growth to bottom in a couple of quarters as the stronger bookings trajectory flows through revenue."

articles.body: BENGALURU: Enterprise AI company Fractal Analytics reported a 139% year-on-year increase in net profit to Rs 79.2 crore for the September quarter, compared with Rs 33.2 crore a year earlier, helped by growth in its healthcare and financial services businesses and improved operating profitability.The company’s total income rose about 20% to Rs 985.3 crore from Rs 819.4 crore a year ago, marking Fractal’s first quarter with revenue exceeding $100 million.Healthcare and life sciences was the fastest-growing business, with revenue rising 79% year-on-year. The segment accounted for 25.1% of quarterly revenue. Banking, financial services and insurance grew 30%, contributing another 13.6%.Fractal’s largest business, serving consumer goods and retail companies, grew 11% and accounted for nearly 35% of revenue. However, its technology, media and telecom business recorded an 18% year-on-year decline, although revenue recovered 6% from the preceding quarter.The Americas continued to account for the bulk of Fractal’s business, contributing 67.3% of revenue, followed by Europe at 21.5%. Revenue from these regions grew 22% and 20%, respectively.Fractal’s adjusted operating profit rose 30% to Rs 154.9 crore from Rs 119.5 crore, with margins improving to 16.2% from 15%. However, its gross profit margin narrowed to 44% from 46.2%, as spending on AI engineering talent increased.The sharp rise in net profit also came as employee stock option and retention bonus expenses declined to Rs 4.8 crore from Rs 22.6 crore. Finance costs fell to Rs 5.3 crore from Rs 11.5 crore.Fractal’s AI products business, which includes its Cogentiq platform, recorded 39% revenue growth to Rs 38.3 crore. The business contributed 4% of group revenue and added eight clients during the quarter. Its annualised revenue run-rate crossed Rs 150 crore.The company also expanded its relationships with large customers. The number of clients generating more than $1 million in annual revenue increased to 58 from 52 a year earlier. Those contributing over $20 million rose to six from four.“AI models are getting more capable every week and cheaper every quarter,” said Srikanth Velamakanni, co-founder and group CEO. “Within the next few quarters, we will cross a threshold where it becomes irresponsible and downright risky for companies to leave their most important decisions unchanged.”Fractal had cash and investments worth Rs 1,727.7 crore at the end of September, including Rs 607.8 crore in net IPO proceeds. articles.title: Stocks shrugged off the blue wave overnight — history says don't trust the bounce yet
articles.summary: Wall Street bought the blue wave by sunrise, but a broken midterm pattern and weak chip stocks say the bounce may not last.
articles.body:
Stock futures tumbled as Democrats swept Congress, then roared back before sunrise, with the Dow ( ^DJI ) on track for its best day since April 8. History says the bounce is easy and the next few weeks are harder.

Election night went the way polls and prediction markets said it would. Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate, and futures slid as the results rolled in. Tech took the worst of it after a Democrat won the Texas governor's race on a promise to halt new data center construction.

Then the buyers showed up, with small caps leading the way.

Don't get too attached. Big reversals feel decisive in the moment, but they haven't said much about what comes next. Since 1997, when S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) futures fell at least 1% during a session and then closed up 1% or more, the following week was about as likely to rise as any other week, according to Yahoo Finance calculations. After the biggest reversals, where futures erased a drop of 2% or more, they fell the next day nearly two out of three times.

Stocks have seen this movie before. On election night in 2016, S&P 500 futures plunged 5% and hit their limit down, then closed higher the next day. TKer editor and founder Sam Ro drew the same comparison Wednesday and warned against rushing to conclusions based on a couple of hours of trading.

The less cheerful precedent is 2018, the last time President Trump lost the House. Stocks rallied about 2% the day after that midterm, then fell about 6% over the next month on the way to a Christmas Eve low.

Small caps also deserve a reality check. The Russell 2000 ( ^RUT ) beat the S&P 500 the day after the vote in only 5 of the past 11 midterms. The season that has favored small caps doesn't start until mid-December.

Stocks went into Election Day in a hole. The eight sessions around a midterm vote, five before and three after, have been one of the S&P 500's strongest stretches of the year , with gains in 18 of 19 midterms since 1950.

This year's window opened at the Oct. 27 close, and the index was down 2% through Tuesday. That's already a steeper loss than any full window since at least 1950, including 1994's 1.3% drop, the only previous loser. To avoid becoming the second losing window in that stretch, the S&P 500 needs to climb about 2% from Tuesday's close by Friday's close.

When a pattern that reliable breaks down, it's worth asking why. The only time the window lost money, in 1994, the Federal Reserve was raising rates. In 2018, another hiking year, the S&P 500 slid about 13% from the end of October to Christmas Eve.

articles.title: Lenskart net profit surges 125% to Rs 232 cr in Q2
articles.summary: Lenskart Q2 FY27 net profit jumps 125% to Rs 232 crore; income up 36% to Rs 2,899 crore on higher sales, margins, and store expansion.
articles.body: BENGALURU: Eyewear retailer Lenskart reported a 125% year-on-year increase in its net profit to Rs 232 crore for the September quarter of FY27, compared with Rs 103 crore a year earlier, as higher eyewear sales and improved margins boosted earnings.Total income rose 36.2% to Rs 2,899 crore from Rs 2,129 crore in the year-ago quarter.Lenskart separately reported profit growth of 106% and revenue growth of 32.5% on a pro forma basis, which adjusts the previous year’s figures to account for acquisitions. These management-prepared comparisons have not been reviewed by auditors.The company’s India business recorded a 35.3% rise in revenue to Rs 1,668 crore, helped by higher sales volumes and growing demand for premium lenses. It sold 85.5 lakh eyewear units in India during the quarter, up 26.5% from a year earlier.The average selling price in India increased 6.9% to Rs 1,950, as more customers bought premium and progressive lenses. Sales at stores operational for at least a year grew 20.8%, compared with 14.8% in the corresponding quarter last year.Lenskart added 143 stores in India during the quarter, including 94 in tier-II and smaller markets, and entered 61 new cities. Its domestic network now spans 2,868 stores across 665 cities.The company also conducted 80 lakh eye tests globally during the quarter, an increase of 40.4%. Of these, 70 lakh were conducted in India, with more than half being first-time eye examinations.International revenue rose 29.5% to Rs 1,201 crore, supported by growth in Japan, Southeast Asia and the Middle East. Excluding currency movements, international revenue grew around 23%. The company added 22 stores overseas, taking its total global store count to 3,624.Lenskart’s operating profit, excluding the impact of lease accounting, increased 65% to Rs 392 crore. Its operating margin improved to 13.8% from 11.1% a year earlier.The company said greater in-house manufacturing helped protect margins despite the rupee’s depreciation against the Chinese yuan. Production of frames at its own facilities increased nearly 72%, while lens manufacturing grew 52%.In India, marketing expenditure declined to 4.5% of revenue from 5.4% a year earlier. However, the company said the reduction partly reflected the timing of spending and that it intended to increase investment in brand building.Lenskart is also expanding its manufacturing capacity, with a new Hyderabad facility designed to produce five crore pairs of eyewear annually expected to be ready in about a year.For the first half of FY27, the company reported revenue of Rs 5,559 crore and net profit of Rs 461 crore. articles.title: Oil prices drop below $100 as midterms fuel hope for an end to the Iran war
articles.summary: Oil prices dropped sharply Wednesday, propelled by growing hopes for a resolution in the Iran war.
articles.body: Oil prices dropped sharply Wednesday, propelled by growing hopes for a resolution in the Iran war. European Brent crude fell below $100 per barrel for the first time since Oct. 7. The move translated to a nearly $8 drop, or an 8.3% decline. U.S. crude oil, or West Texas Intermediate, also slipped 8.3% to close at about $88.12. It was oil’s biggest daily decline since April. Relief for consumers may follow. Oil’s fall could bring the national average price of gas down below $4 in the “days ahead,” Patrick De Haan, an analyst at GasBuddy, said. Prices moved lower as trading desks and energy experts watched closely for a sign that Tuesday’s midterm election results would pressure President Donald Trump into ending the Iran war without a major escalation. The war sent gasoline and diesel prices skyrocketing, making already stubborn inflation worse for American consumers, farmers and business owners. “The next six weeks typically deliver one of the most hostile environments for higher gasoline and diesel prices,” Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser to Gulf Oil, said on social media. “If the US or Iran don’t pursue ‘scorched earth’ policies in the Persian Gulf, we may see considerably lower prices by second half December.” On Wednesday morning, that average price was $4.12. That’s 39% higher than before Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu launched the Iran war Feb. 28, which snarled shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. On social media, Vice President JD Vance said the war is the reason the Republican Party suffered such steep losses in the midterm elections. “And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there,” said Vance, who could be the GOP’s standard-bearer in the 2028 presidential election. Trump also said he realized the toll the Iran war took on American consumers. “I think it’s the gasoline price,” Trump said Tuesday night on Fox News as the first results became clear. “People agree with what I’m doing on Iran, but they really probably weren’t willing to do the short-term consequence of paying more for gasoline, and that, you know, I understand that.” Oil’s drop over the last three trading sessions has been precipitous. On Friday, Brent oil traded as high as $118 per barrel, but by Wednesday, its price was around $94. Despite the sharp move lower, the overall price of oil remains higher by 60% compared with the start of the year. On Tuesday, 59% of voters who went to the ballot box told NBC News in an exit poll that they were “very concerned” with the cost of gas and diesel fuel, echoing concerns that consumers have voiced for months. But diesel fuel prices have economists far more concerned. U.S. diesel futures also tumbled Wednesday. As of midday, prices declined by nearly 7%, to their lowest level since the end of August. That likely means that more relief is coming for prices at the pump. As the fuel that powers transportation services for goods, such as groceries, across the country, any jump in prices could quickly ripple across the economy through higher prices on store shelves.

articles.title: Stock futures soar after Democratic rout in midterms
articles.summary: Stock futures soared Wednesday morning, after Democrats’ resounding victory in the midterms. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures were up roughly 1,150 points before the opening bell, more than 2 percent higher than closing time Tuesday. S&P 500 and Nasdaq composite futures were up by more than 90 and 120 points, respectively. As of the late…
articles.body:
Stock futures soared Wednesday morning , after Democrats’ resounding victory in the midterms.

Dow Jones Industrial Average futures were up roughly 1,150 points before the opening bell, more than 2 percent higher than closing time Tuesday. S&P 500 and Nasdaq composite futures were up by more than 90 and 120 points, respectively.

As of the late morning, Dow Jones, S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures were respectively up by 1,416 points, 117 points and 290 points.

Democrats flipped the House, Senate and multiple governor’s mansions in Tuesday’s elections , breaking up the GOP’s grip on Congress and dealing a political blow to President Trump.

“Wall Street loves divided government, because typically divided government doesn’t do anything, and it’s very much the case in this particular situation that it’s going to be very hard to do anything affirmative during the last two years of Trump’s administration,” Daniel Alpert, the executive chair at Westwood Capital, told The Hill.

Liz Ann Sonders, the chief investment strategist at the Schwab Center for Financial Research, argued Wednesday on Schwab Network the “decisive” nature of the election allowed investors to “look forward” to what’s in store for the economy.

Democrats across the map campaigned on affordability issues, blaming Trump and Republicans for high gas prices amid the Iran war and persistent inflation . That paid off, as Decision Desk HQ has called 249 House and 54 Senate seats for Democrats as of midday Wednesday.

Voters also soundly rejected the explosion in data center construction. Of the 44 measures on the issue, voters backed restricting construction in 37 instances, with the restrict position leading in six other cases, according to data from Redbud Consulting.

Democrats, such as Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown in Ohio and Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa in Texas, campaigned on reining in the AI build-out. Investors took notice, as shares of tech companies like Nvidia and Elon Musk’s SpaceX were down as of late Wednesday morning.

“The AI industry has clearly benefited from a hands-off approach by the Trump administration, which is very unlikely to be continued by a Democratic Congress,” Alpert noted.

If the AI industry experiences a “disruption” from the next Congress, the gains in stock futures will reverse, Alpert argued.

“Long story is it’s a pop,” Alpert, who noted he has shorted the market, said of stock futures surging. “People are going to buy into that pop because the divided government argument, and then we’re going to see what really happens.”

Bond yields also dipped in the aftermath of Democrats’ resounding victories. The 10- and 30-year U.S. Treasury bond yields were down by roughly 4 and 3 basis points, respectively, as of the late morning.

The notes have climbed this year , as the federal government’s mounting debt and a rise in oil prices amid the Iran war led to a sell-off.

On the campaign trail, Democrats vowed to lower prices by restricting Trump’s tariff authorities , forcing him to wind down the Middle Eastern conflict and tackling rising healthcare costs.

Sonders argued that if lawmakers are able to bring down costs, their actions will seep into the markets.

“To the extent that there is success in bringing the cost of living down, which is how constituents typically categorize, what we categorize as inflation and the various metrics measuring that … I think it would generally be seen as a positive for both the economy and the equity market,” she said.

Alpert said, however, that Trump could derail the stock futures’ “pop” during the lame-duck session. The president told Politico’s Dasha Burns on Tuesday night he will “ take a look ” at the potential next steps in the war, which is in its eighth month.

Roughly 6 in 10 voters said Trump made the wrong decision to take military action against Iran, according to NBC News exit polling .

Despite voters rebuking the president and Republicans over the war, Alpert noted Trump could “assert himself in ways that nobody can really anticipate” until the next Congress.

“Oil, I believe, will actually likely resolve itself fairly quickly unless [Trump] starts dropping bombs,” Alpert said.

articles.summary: The referendum would amend California's constitution and impose a one-time 5% tax on California residents and trusts with assets over $1 billion.
articles.body:
California's proposed billionaire tax appeared headed for defeat on Wednesday in one of the final verdicts from voters in an election week that saw a wave of anti-billionaire sentiment elsewhere.

The latest results on Wednesday afternoon showed California's Proposition 40 down by over 11 percentage points, with 60% of votes counted but the race not yet formally called.

The referendum would amend California's constitution and impose a one-time 5% tax on California residents and trusts with assets over $1 billion on Jan. 1, 2026. The revenue would primarily go toward healthcare, as well as food assistance and education.

Some assets, such as real property and certain retirement accounts and pensions, were excluded.

The measure was estimated to impact about 200 billionaires in the state. It faced fierce opposition from many in Big Tech and lost steam with voters as Election Day neared.

Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ) co-founder Sergey Brin was one of the measure's most vocal opponents. He contributed a reported $102 million to a political committee to fight the measure.

Other billionaires made detailed plans in case it passed. Meta ( META ) CEO Mark Zuckerberg told his board, according to a New York Times report, that they needed to take steps to shield him from the tax or he would publicly list his home in Palo Alto for sale.

The measure was also opposed by some Democrats, who argued it wouldn't work.

Outgoing California Gov. Gavin Newsom emerged as an opponent, arguing that billionaires would both dodge the tax and leave the state. He cited a report from the California Legislative Analyst's Office that estimated the measure might temporarily boost state revenues but could be an overall drag on regular income taxes and "would reduce state revenues by less than $1 billion per year."

Across the country, voters in red and blue states delivered verdicts on wealth inequality and the influence of the ultrarich. In Texas, where Elon Musk spent more than $200 million to keep the state's Senate seat in Republican hands, voters flipped the seat for Democrats and made clear their unease over AI data centers .

Tuesday's results also saw a series of wins by candidates who represent the Democratic Socialists of America , many of whom ran on explicitly anti-billionaire platforms. At least seven DSA members will take seats in Congress next year, as well as the mayors' offices of Los Angeles and Washington, D.C.

California voters were also weighing competing measures: Proposition 41 and Proposition 42 , which were introduced by opponents of Proposition 40 to prevent the wealth tax from taking effect.

articles.title: Oil prices fall below $90 as traders bet on Iran war ending after Democrats sweep midterms
articles.summary: Crude is on track for its worst week since 2020 as traders bet the Iran war is winding down.
articles.body:
Wall Street's post-midterm party has two no-shows: AI and chip stocks, and oil. Crude is having the far worse time, on track for its worst week since April 2020.

West Texas Intermediate crude ( CL=F ) settled at $88.12 a barrel on Wednesday, down more than 8% on the day and $16 below Friday's close of $104. Its three-day drop of about 15% is its steepest since November 2021.

Brent ( BZ=F ), the global benchmark, is near a two-month low. The sell-off came as traders bet on an end to the Iran war after Democrats swept Tuesday's elections.

"The election results may pressure the president to seek to end the war more quickly," the Wells Fargo Investment Institute wrote Wednesday.

The damage is spreading beyond crude. Gasoline futures ( RB=F ) are on track for their lowest close since March 10, which is good news for anyone driving to Thanksgiving dinner. The Energy Select Sector SPDR Fund ( XLE ) is down more than 5%. Refiners Marathon Petroleum ( MPC ) and Valero ( VLO ) are down about 8% to 10%.

Even after the slide, oil hasn't given back the whole war. WTI started 2026 near $57 and peaked near $113 on April 7, and it's still roughly 50% above where the year began.

The election angle adds some history. Oil hasn't followed a single script after Trump's elections. Crude rose about 10% from Election Day through the end of November after his 2016 win and about 20% after his 2020 loss, and it fell about 6% after his 2024 win.

The closest echo is 2018, Trump's first midterm, when Democrats took the House. Crude fell about 18% from Election Day through the end of that November, by Yahoo Finance calculations.

Supply hasn't caught up with the peace trade. US diesel stockpiles are at their lowest since 2003, and Wells Fargo noted that gasoline and diesel supplies "remain constrained by the war."

That leaves crude priced for a deal that hasn't happened. Nationwide's chief market strategist, Mark Hackett, says oil is retreating "on hopes for a deescalation in the Iran conflict, even as the diplomatic signals remain ambiguous."

articles.title: 3M stock soars following $7.35 billion 'forever chemicals' settlement
articles.summary: By Jonathan Stempel, Anshuman Tripathy and Vallari Srivastava Nov 4 (Reuters) - Shares of 3M hit an 8-1/2-year high on Wednesday after the industrial product...
articles.body:
By Jonathan Stempel, Anshuman Tripathy and Vallari Srivastava

Nov 4 (Reuters) - Shares of 3M hit an 8-1/2-year high on Wednesday after the industrial products company agreed to pay $7.35 billion to settle litigation by people ‌who said its "forever chemicals" injured them, and 3M officials predicted enough claimants would join for the ‌settlement to take effect.

Payouts would cover personal injury claims related to firefighting foam made by 3M and be distributed over nine years to ​as many as 120,000 people, the St. Paul, Minnesota-based company said on Wednesday. It announced the settlement on Tuesday after US markets closed.

The litigation centers on PFAS, short for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, in products manufactured by 3M.

"Forever chemicals" do not break down easily in the human body or environment, and have been linked to health issues including higher ‌cholesterol, low birth weight and kidney and ⁠testicular cancer.

The company did not admit liability, and plans a $5.8 billion pre-tax fourth-quarter charge that represents the present value of future payments.

UBS analyst Amit Mehrotra wrote that investors had expected an ⁠approximately $10 billion settlement, and the accord removes a "meaningful overhang" on 3M's shares.

At its peak, 3M stock rose 10% on Wednesday to its highest since March 2018, when it traded above $200. In afternoon trading, the shares were up 9.8% at $194.37.

The settlement ​addresses about ​99% of personal injury claims inside and outside the "aqueous film-forming ​foam" multi-district litigation in the federal court in ‌Charleston, South Carolina.

JUDGE URGES 'SIGNIFICANT TIME AND EFFORT'

Kevin Rhodes, 3M's chief legal affairs officer, said on a conference call on Wednesday that the settlement is designed to address current and future PFAS claims, and 3M will pay most of the money between 2028 and 2033.

Rhodes said 3M can walk away if not enough claimants accept the settlement, "although we do not expect that to happen."

US District Judge Richard Gergel on Wednesday stayed personal injury proceedings against 3M in ‌the litigation, saying the company and claimants should devote "significant time and ​effort" to implementing the settlement.

In a joint statement, plaintiffs' lawyers David ​Hoyle and Fred Thompson said the settlement benefits ​thousands of people who "sought answers and accountability" for nearly a decade.

Foam has often been used ‌to put out high-intensity fires, including on military ​bases and at airports.

PFAS in ​firefighters' protective gear has also included 3M's Scotchlite reflective material.

articles.summary: Markets priced in a divided government and assessed what a Democratic sweep of midterm elections means for key industries.
articles.body: US stocks jumped on Wednesday after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in a seismic midterm election, paving the way for a divided government.The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) rose 3%, or over 1,500 points, marking its best single-day performance since President Trump paused a sweeping tariff rollout in April 2025. The S&P 500 (^GSPC) climbed 1.6%. The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) traded up by 1.4% amid a post-election relief rally.Markets swiftly repriced a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate — and the potential for ballot measures and newly elected officials to restrict data center construction. Chip stocks, including Nvidia (NVDA) and Micron (MU), fell. Meanwhile, other parts of the tech sector offset some of those losses, with Apple (AAPL) and Microsoft (MSFT) each hitting all-time highs.Oil prices plunged as the midterm election outcome also raised hopes for an end to the war in the Middle East. Brent crude oil futures (BZ=F) dropped 8% to around $95 per barrel.Investors will also be watching in the coming weeks for policy actions on housing and pharmaceuticals in the aftermath of the election. As Yahoo Finance's Jared Blikre pointed out on Tuesday, midterm elections have a history of shaping stock performance in the near term but don't tend to move markets much over the long term. On the economic front, ISM and S&P data showed that US services activity expanded at a slower pace in October as businesses continued to grapple with elevated costs. Private-sector hiring, meanwhile, continued to show strength in October as an ADP report indicated "pretty solid job growth."Earnings continue to roll in. AMD (AMD) posted a Q3 earnings beat, while McDonald's (MCD) grappled with slowing same-store sales growth. Duolingo (DUOL) stock soared over 30% on strong user growth.

articles.title: Qualcomm tops Q4 estimates, but Q1 earnings outlook falls short
articles.summary: Qualcomm reported its Q4 earnings after the bell Wednesday.
articles.body:
Qualcomm ( QCOM ) reported fourth quarter earnings after the bell Wednesday, topping expectations on the top and bottom lines and providing a better-than-anticipated Q1 revenue outlook.

But a lower-than-expected midpoint for its earnings per share (EPS) forecast sent the stock lower following the report.

For Q4, Qualcomm reported adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $2.17 on revenue of $10.32 billion. Analysts were projecting EPS of $2.16 and revenue of $10.12 billion.

The company saw EPS of $3 and revenue of $11.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Qualcomm also offered Q1 revenue guidance of $10.4 billion to $11.2 billion, with the midpoint ahead of Wall Street's $10.6 billion outlook.

EPS, however, is set to come in between $2.15 and $2.35, with a midpoint of $2.25. Analysts were looking for $2.32

Qualcomm's QCT segment, which includes handset and automotive sales, declined 8% year over year but topped Wall Street's Q4 expectations on revenue of $9 billion. Analysts were calling for $8.8 billion.

The bulk of that drop came from Qualcomm's handset business, which saw revenue plunge 26% year over year to $5.1 billion. Analysts were looking for $5.3 billion.

But the company's automotive segment helped offset some of that impact, with sales increasing 89% to $2 billion.

Qualcomm's QTL business line saw revenue of $1.3 billion for the quarter.

The chip giant is in the midst of a wide-ranging effort to bolster its data center, automotive, edge computing, and PC businesses, as it works to reduce its dependence on smartphone chip sales.

On Wednesday, Qualcomm announced a deal to provide technology to SpaceX's ( SPCX ) Starlink as the satellite networking giant ramps up its effort to establish a terrestrial network that would rival AT&T ( T ), T-Mobile ( TMUS ), and Verizon ( VZ ).

In late October, Qualcomm said it is working with Anduril on a product line called BlueChip focused on reshoring computer manufacturing. The companies say they'll start by focusing on a laptop that will use Qualcomm's Snapdragon X series chips.

And in September, the company signed an agreement with Amazon for custom chips designed for its AWS AI infrastructure.

But Qualcomm, like the rest of the consumer electronics industry, is also contending with the impact of the memory and storage shortage, which has forced companies to raise prices on everything from smartphones to laptops, sending demand plummeting.

During its fourth quarter earnings announcement on Monday, Apple noted that the memory crisis will continue to cut into margins going forward. Intel ( INTC ) and AMD ( AMD ) also said they expect PC sales to decline in the coming quarter, sending shares of Intel plunging nearly 29% .

articles.title: Snapchat surpasses 30M paid subscribers
articles.summary: The milestone comes a year after Snapchat announced a controversial limit on free storage for its Memories feature and informed users it would start requirin...
articles.body:
Snap has surpassed 30 million paid Snapchat+ subscribers, the company announced Wednesday in its third-quarter 2026 earnings release . The milestone marks an increase of 5 million subscribers since February, when Snap reported crossing the 25 million mark .

Launched in 2022, Snapchat+ gives subscribers access to exclusive and pre-release features for $3.99 per month. Following a successful launch, Snap introduced additional paid tiers beyond the core Snapchat+ subscription to further diversify its revenue streams. These include Lens+, an $8.99-per-month plan that unlocks exclusive Lenses and AR experiences, and Snapchat+ Platinum, a $15.99 monthly tier that offers an ad-free experience.

The milestone comes a year after Snapchat announced a controversial limit on free storage for its Memories feature and informed users it would start requiring users to pay $1.99 per month for additional storage or subscribe to Snapchat+ to retain their Memories.

"We surpassed 30 million paid subscribers across Snapchat+, Memories Storage, and Lens+," Snap CEO Evan Spiegel said in a letter to investors. "Innovative AI-powered features have helped Lens+ exceed our expectations, demonstrating how new creative experiences can drive demand for our paid products. Paid subscribers still represent a small share of our monthly community, giving us room to grow through broader adoption and new premium experiences."

As for the company's broader earnings release, Snap's shares fell 12% after missing ad revenue and user growth estimates.

Snap reported 495 million daily active users for the quarter, up from 493 million in the previous quarter. However, the figure fell short of analysts' expectations of 499 million.

"Daily engagement has historically been stable as a percentage of monthly engagement, but we do not intend to optimize Snapchat around daily use at the expense of long-term value for our community," the investor letter said. "A longer-term horizon better aligns our reported metrics with the product and safety decisions that strengthen relationships, create lasting utility, and support broader, more durable audience growth."

Spiegel said in the letter than while advertising revenue growth remains below the company's target, the company plans to prioritize improving advertiser performance and expanding the ways businesses can reach its users.

articles.title: Democrats just broke GOP’s grip on Texas. What comes next?
articles.summary: A seismic political shift occurred in Texas on Tuesday, as Democrats flipped a Senate seat and the governor’s mansion in a traditionally conservative stronghold. With Sen.-elect James Talarico’s double-digit victory over state Attorney General Ken Paxton and Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa’s upset win over three-term Gov. Greg Abbott (R), Democrats broke the GOP’s grip on the…
articles.body:
A seismic political shift occurred in Texas on Tuesday, as Democrats flipped a Senate seat and the governor’s mansion in a traditionally conservative stronghold.

With Sen.-elect James Talarico’s double-digit victory over state Attorney General Ken Paxton and Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa’s upset win over three-term Gov. Greg Abbott (R), Democrats broke the GOP’s grip on the second-most populous state in the country.

The results shift Texas, which Republicans have long touted as a business-friendly alternative for companies looking to flee Democratic-run California, from a reliably red state to a place where Democrats can win statewide.

“I think Texas, like South Carolina and like the entire South, is pregnant with possibility,” Democratic strategist Antjuan Seawright told The Hill.

Prior to Tuesday, a Democrat had not won a Texas gubernatorial race since former Gov. Ann Richards in 1990. The party’s dry spell in Texas Senate races was even longer, as former Sen. Lloyd Bentsen in 1988 was the last Democrat from the Lone Star State elected to the upper chamber.

During that time, Texas transitioned from a purple state to one where Republicans could reliably expect to win statewide races.

That paid dividends for business interests. Texas has the most oil refineries of any state in the country, with 29, according to data from Apollo Technical. That is 15 more than Louisiana, the next-closest state.

Under Abbott, Texas also became a destination for companies across industries. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, Charles Schwab, Chevron, Oracle, SpaceX and Tesla have moved to the Lone Star State from California, with company leaders often citing the business-friendly environment and lower taxes in Texas.

That included Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX and Tesla. Musk, the richest man in the world, directed $158 million to the Paxton-aligned Texas PAC last month.

That bet did not pay off, as Talarico campaigned on reining in the influence of wealthy donors and billionaires on politics en route to a comfortable victory over the state attorney general.

During his victory speech, the incoming senator referenced Musk, saying he took on “the richest man in the world” and comparing himself to the underdog David who defeated Goliath.

“We just sent a message to every billionaire mega-donor, every trillionaire mega-donor, every corrupt defender of this broken political system. In this state, in this country, power belongs to the people,” Talarico remarked .

Hinojosa spoke in a similar tone Tuesday, saying her victory proved Texas was “by and for the people” and did not “belong” to billionaires.

“Does Texas belong to the farmers and ranchers who have worked this land for generations, or the corporations trying to buy it up?” she said, referencing the dynamics of her race against Abbott.

The strong night for Democrats in Texas did not apply solely to Talarico and Hinojosa. Democratic state Rep. Vikki Goodwin defeated Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick (R), while Democrats won the races for state attorney general, comptroller, railroad commissioner and agriculture commissioner.

Democrats also captured the Texas state House, ending Republicans’ 24-year run in charge of both state Legislature chambers.

Saul Elbein, a native Texan who runs the nonprofit energy industry watchdog Future Heist , argued statewide Democratic victories will not usher in a new era of restrictions on business.

Elbein told The Hill that while companies attempting to build data centers “may have a harder time” with Hinojosa in the governor’s mansion, businesses will benefit from Democrats focusing on economic issues.

“I think the new group of people who have come in are, at the very least, deeply serious about governance in a way that I think is a return to what business is looking for, even if they would prefer to pay lower taxes,” added Elbein, also a former reporter for The Hill.

Pundits and politicians cited a variety of factors for the blue earthquake in Texas , which came as Democrats flipped the House , Senate and multiple governor’s mansions across the country .

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), who lost the GOP primary to the scandal-plagued Paxton earlier this year, said the results show “character and integrity still matter” to voters.

“Here in Texas, traditional conservatives and independents were asked to swallow an almost comical list of personal scandals and improprieties,” Cornyn wrote in a Wall Street Journal op-ed published Wednesday.

Seawright cited economic concerns, referencing the impact of high diesel prices on farmers and cattle ranchers in Texas. The price of diesel has soared during the Iran war , with a gallon costing roughly $2.51 more on average than it did a year ago in Texas, according to AAA .

Doug Heye, the former communications director for the Republican National Committee, faulted President Trump. The GOP strategist said Tuesday’s results stemmed from a “totally self-created Trump Quake” which acted “as an albatross that smothered Republicans” across the country.

“Add to that good smart Democratic candidates like Talarico and Hinojosa and Trump created the perfect Democratic storm,” Heye added via email.

Whether that “storm” signals Texas being consistently competitive in statewide races is unclear, Seawright acknowledged.

The Democratic strategist noted that “no coalition is forever,” saying his party will have to “expand on” what Talarico, Hinojosa and other Democrats pulled off “every single cycle” going forward.

Elbein, though, said he could “absolutely see” a Democrat winning Texas in the 2028 presidential election — if the party delivers on its promises to voters.

“I don’t see any particular reason, based on the numbers in the electorate, why Texas wouldn’t be in play,” he noted.

articles.title: Exit polling shows electorate still frustrated with prices
articles.summary: Welcome to The Hill’s Business & Economy newsletter {beacon} Business & Economy Business & Economy The Big Story Exit polling shows electorate still frustrated with prices A wave of exit polls from the midterms had a common theme: Americans remain frustrated with inflation, and blamed President Trump and Republicans for persistently high prices. ©…
articles.body:
Exit polling shows electorate still frustrated with prices

A wave of exit polls from the midterms had a common theme: Americans remain frustrated with inflation, and blamed President Trump and Republicans for persistently high prices.

© Stephanie Scarbrough, Associated Press

Two years after Trump and the GOP rode Americans’ frustrations over inflation to unified control of government, Democrats flipped the switch on Tuesday, snatching control of both chambers of Congress after campaigning on affordability.

Nearly 9 in 10 voters said the cost of living was either a “crucial” or “major” factor in who they voted for, based on NBC News exit polling. Three-fourths of voters also told NBC News the country’s economy is “not so good” or “poor.”

Trump promised to tackle inflation in 2024, after it hit a 40-year high two years earlier. But inflation has risen above 3.5 percent this fall, as the Iran war’s spillover effects keeps fuel prices elevated.

Exit polling shows Americans are dissatisfied with Trump’s handling of the economy. Forty-four percent of voters that CBS News surveyed said their financial situation is worse than it was two years ago, while 38 percent said it was about the same and 18 percent said it was better.

“We know that pocketbook pain and pressure was a … big driver of the turnout and the enthusiasm last night,” Democratic strategist Antjuan Seawright told The Hill on Wednesday.

Seawright, a senior adviser to the Democratic National Committee, argued that the results give Democrats a chance to make a positive impact on voters’ lives in the form of legislation.

That legislation should center around issues that have “bipartisan” support from Americans, he said, including reining in Trump’s tariff authority and forcing him to wind down the Iran conflict.

“I think we have to deal with matters that impact the material well-being of everyday Americans. … Whether it’s gas, groceries [or] housing,” he said.
